name: Speculative Decoding
question: Can a small model draft tokens for the big one?
summary: A fast draft model proposes several tokens ahead. The large target model checks them all in a single forward pass and keeps the longest correct prefix, supplying its own token at the first mismatch. With the standard acceptance rule the output matches what the target model would have produced alone. Reported speed-ups are typically around 2–3×.
useCases: Interactive products where tokens per second matters
Long outputs such as code, reports and documents
Edits that copy large parts of the input (prompt lookup)

items.detail: a small model, or extra heads (Medusa, EAGLE)
the target scores all drafted tokens in parallel
draft by copying n-grams from the prompt

steps: Pick a draft that shares the target’s tokenizer
Measure acceptance rate on your real prompts
Tune lookahead k; too high wastes verification work
Use prompt-lookup decoding for code edits that repeat the input
pitfalls: A low acceptance rate gives little or even negative speed-up
The draft model needs extra GPU memory
Gains shrink at large batch sizes, when the GPU is already busy
remember: Draft fast, verify in one pass.
caption: Accepted tokens are free extra output. The first mismatch is replaced by the target’s own token.

code.text: preds = big.greedy_all(tokens + draft)   # 1 pass, k+1 predictions
out.append(preds[k])                # all k accepted: bonus token

steps.title: Draft k tokens cheaply
steps.text: The small draft model proposes k = 4 tokens one after another. Each draft step costs a small fraction of a target pass.

steps.title: Verify all of them in one pass
steps.text: The target model runs once over the prompt plus the 4 drafts and produces its own prediction at every position, 5 in total.

steps.title: Accept the longest matching prefix
steps.text: “five” and “business” match the target’s predictions, so both are kept. This sketch uses greedy matching; with sampling, a probabilistic rule keeps the target’s distribution exactly.

steps.title: Replace the first mismatch
steps.text: The target wanted “days”, not “weeks”. Its token is used and the rest of the draft is discarded: 3 new tokens from one target pass.

steps.title: Measure acceptance
steps.text: Count accepted drafts against drafts checked. Over this run the per-token acceptance rate α is 0.70; on real prompts it is the number that decides everything.

steps.title: Estimate the speed-up
steps.text: With k = 4 and α = 0.7, a pass yields (1 − 0.7⁵) ÷ 0.3 ≈ 2.77 tokens. Dividing by the cost 1 + 4 × 0.05 = 1.2 gives about 2.3×.

playgroundGuide.scenario: A self-hosted model generates trade-confirmation summaries at 40 tokens per second with plain decoding. You are testing speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes k tokens, and the target model checks them all in one pass. The output is unchanged; only speed changes. Numbers use the standard expected-tokens formula, (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α).
controls: Set the acceptance rate α: how often the target agrees with a drafted token.
Set lookahead k and the draft’s cost per token, relative to one target pass.
Choose the batch size: on a busy GPU, verifying extra tokens stops being free.

outputs.name: Speed-up

presets.name: Busy GPU

missions.hint: Raise the acceptance rate first; a well-matched draft matters more than a long lookahead.

practice.scenario: A self-hosted model writes trade-confirmation summaries and code edits. Adding speculative decoding with a small draft model from the same family raises tokens per second, and because every drafted token is checked by the main model, the output stays the same.

industries.use: Prompt-lookup drafting speeds up edits that copy the input
Faster long summaries on self-hosted GPUs

practice.analogy: A junior drafts the next few lines of a letter; the senior reads them at a glance, keeps what's right and fixes the first mistake.

library.name: vLLM
library.what: The most widely used open-source inference server. Speculative decoding is a config option: a draft model, n-gram lookup, or EAGLE heads.

samples.code:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct",
    tensor_parallel_size=4,
    speculative_config={
        "model": "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct",   # draft: same tokenizer family
        "num_speculative_tokens": 5,                    # lookahead k
    },
)
out = llm.generate(["Summarize this trade confirmation: ..."],
                   SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=300))
print(out[0].outputs[0].text)

# For code edits, draft from the prompt itself (no draft model needed):
# speculative_config={"method": "ngram", "num_speculative_tokens": 5,
#                     "prompt_lookup_max": 4}

numericDrill.question: Lookahead k = 4. On average 3 drafted tokens are accepted per step, plus 1 token from the target. A target pass costs 1 unit and the draft costs 0.1 per token. Tokens per unit of cost?
numericDrill.answer: Plain decoding: 1 token per unit. Speculative: 4 tokens per (1 + 4 × 0.1) = 1.4 units ≈ 2.86 tokens per unit, about 2.9× faster.

interview.question: Why doesn't speculative decoding change the output?
interview.answer: The target model checks every drafted token, and the acceptance rule keeps the output distribution identical to the target's own. Rejected tokens are replaced by the target's choice, so only speed changes.

interview.question: When does speculative decoding help least?
interview.answer: When acceptance is low (a mismatched draft, creative high-temperature sampling), at large batch sizes where the GPU is already busy, or when the draft adds significant memory pressure.

mistakes.mistake: A draft model with a different tokenizer
mistakes.fix: Pick a draft from the same model family
Tune k on real prompts by acceptance rate

quiz.question: Why does speculative decoding not change the model’s output?
options: The draft model is trained to be perfect
The target model verifies every drafted token, and the acceptance rule keeps its output distribution
quiz.explanation: Rejected tokens are replaced by the target’s own choice, so only speed changes.

quiz.question: Acceptance rate α = 0.6 and lookahead k = 3. How many tokens does one target pass produce on average?
Same settings (2.18 tokens per pass, k = 3). Each draft token costs 0.1 of a target pass. What is the net speed-up?
Where does prompt-lookup (n-gram) drafting work well? Select all that apply.
options: Editing code where most of the file is copied unchanged
Answering questions that quote the provided document
Writing a new poem at high temperature
quiz.explanation: It drafts by copying n-grams from the prompt, so it shines when the output repeats the input.

quiz.question: Measured acceptance is 0.25 and the speed-up is 1.05×. What is the best next step?
options: Use a better-matched draft, such as one from the target’s family or EAGLE heads
quiz.explanation: With low acceptance, a longer lookahead only wastes more drafts. A better draft raises acceptance.

quiz.question: Which are valid ways to produce draft tokens? Select all that apply.
options: A smaller model from the same family
Extra heads on the target, such as Medusa or EAGLE
A model with a different tokenizer, used as is
quiz.explanation: Drafts must use the target’s vocabulary; a different tokenizer cannot be verified token by token without extra work.

quiz.question: Speculative decoding gave 2.4× at batch size 1 but almost nothing at batch size 128. Why?
options: At large batches the GPU is compute-busy, so verifying extra tokens is no longer nearly free
quiz.explanation: The gain comes from spare compute during memory-bound decoding; big batches use it up.

quiz.question: How does Medusa draft tokens?
options: Extra decoding heads on the target that predict several future tokens
quiz.explanation: Medusa adds heads to the target model, so no separate draft model is needed.

quiz.question: What distinguishes EAGLE from a small draft model?
options: It drafts from the target model’s own hidden features
quiz.explanation: Predicting at the feature level gives high acceptance rates.

quiz.question: Plain decoding runs at 30 tokens per second; speculative decoding gives 2.4×. How long does a 600-token claim letter take to generate?
quiz.explanation: 30 × 2.4 = 72 tokens per second; 600 ÷ 72 ≈ 8.3 s, against 20 s.

quiz.question: What should you measure before enabling speculative decoding in production? Select all that apply.
options: Tokens per second at production batch sizes
GPU memory headroom for the draft
The draft model’s public benchmark score
quiz.explanation: Only your prompts and traffic show the real gain. The draft’s own quality score is beside the point.

quiz.question: At α = 0.5, raising k from 2 to 10 raises tokens per pass from 1.75 to about what?
quiz.explanation: (1 − 0.5¹¹) ÷ 0.5 ≈ 2.0. Most extra drafts are rejected, so a long lookahead mostly adds cost.

quiz.question: With sampling at temperature 0.8, how are drafted tokens accepted without changing the output distribution?
options: Only exact matches with the target’s top token are kept
Each is accepted with probability min(1, p_target ÷ p_draft), and on rejection a token is sampled from the adjusted distribution
The draft’s probabilities are used directly
quiz.explanation: This rejection-sampling rule, from the original papers, makes the result distributed exactly as the target’s samples.

quiz.question: A team uses a hosted model API and wants speculative decoding. What is true?
options: They can add a draft model in their client code
It runs inside the inference engine, so they cannot add it themselves, though some providers offer related features such as predicted outputs
It is enabled by setting temperature to 0
quiz.explanation: Speculation happens in the serving engine. Self-hosting or a provider feature is required.

quiz.question: Over a run, 1,200 drafted tokens were accepted out of 1,600 checked. What is the acceptance rate?
Which reduce the benefit of speculative decoding? Select all that apply.
options: A draft whose tokenizer does not match
Long, predictable outputs such as code
quiz.explanation: Long predictable outputs are where it helps most.

quiz.question: In vLLM’s speculative_config, which key sets the lookahead k?
quiz.explanation: num_speculative_tokens is the number of tokens drafted per step.

quiz.question: What are the costs of adding a draft model? Select all that apply.
options: GPU memory for its own KV cache
More settings to tune, such as k
A change in the target’s output
quiz.explanation: Memory and tuning are real costs. The output does not change.

quiz.question: α = 0.9 and k = 4. Expected tokens per target pass?
Time to first token is 3 s and users complain about the wait before anything appears. Will speculative decoding fix it?
options: No: it speeds up decoding, not prefill. Look at prefix caching or prompt length
Yes, if k is large enough
quiz.explanation: The first token waits for prefill. Speculation helps the tokens after it.
